Title: 'Rush Deck NT' (my sucky new Brujah deck)

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
So I was kinda tired of playing my old effective Brujah pot/cel rush
deck, so I turned it into this one for the novelty value of using those
cool Brujah princes and justicars and such. Unfortunately when I played
it for the first time last night I was unceremoniously defeated by hand-
jam, unfortunate vampire draw, and THE CONSPIRACY OF MY PREDATOR AND
PREY TO REMOVE ME FROM THE GAME! Ahem. Sorry about that. ;-)

It went like this: My initial vamp draw was Dr. Dre, Jacob Bragggg,
Jimmy Dunn, and Gwendolyn. I went second. So I put one on each of
Dre and Bragg; my second turn I brought them both out; my third turn
I brought Dunn out. My fourth turn, I paid one to look at another
vamp, knowing that Gwendolyn, while loaded with votes, couldn't play
my 5th Traditions, 2nd traditions, Anathemas, or Archons. Found
Constanza Vinti, exactly what I was looking for. Sadly, before my
fifth turn, I was bled for nine (seven from one vamp, two from another),
reducing me to seven pool and making me unable to get out the necessary
Constanza. Bo.

Now, this didn't have to happen. My predator (Jon Sushinsky) was playing
a Toreador/Anti-Toreador presence bleed deck. He brought out Jost Werner
first, so I pounded him down to 0 blood (but unfortunately not to torpor).
Jon slapped a Blood Doll on him so he could harm me instead of hunting...
Next Jon brought out Alexandra (yipe!). I pounded her into torpor with
Jimmy Dunn before she got to take an action. Tried to bleed to get the
edge and then diablerize, but was blocked bleeding (my prey, Jon Evers,
was playing an anti-Nosferatu combat/intercept/Army of Rats/stuff deck),
so that failed. So then my prey rescued Alexandra from torpor for my
predator, cause he didn't want Jon S to be unable to put pressure on
me. Great. So the next turn, Alexandra gained Blood Doll, a point of
blood, and came to bleed tapped-out me with Social Charm and Aire of
Elation for seven. Plus Jost on the Social Charm for two. Oh look,
now I suck.

Well anyway, so much for my pointless anecdote; I was ultimately ousted
by Jon S Telepathic Misdirecting two stealthy bleeds my way from his
predator (Trey Morita) with the Obf/Pres bleed deck. Oh well.

So the upshot is, I think my deck could have done somewhat better if (a)
I had not had four master cards clog my hand all at once or (b) I had
managed to get out a Prince/Justicar for Minion Tap/5th Traditioning
before being reduced to insufficient pool to start that trick. So
here's the deck. Tell me if you have any good ideas for making it work
better, preferably while preserving the Prince/Justicar angle, although
I'm thinking that maybe I ought to lose the votes (which I may be completely
unable to win in the first place) and stick with just the P/J cards,
maybe add some 3rd Trad: Progeny or something. (The deck was partly
inspired by "Joanie Loves Chachi", but I didn't want to make it a two-vamp
deck. Well, plus I don't have six each of Constanza and Donal. Although
if I did, that might not be completely a bad idea. Oh wait, yes it would.)

crypt (13 vamps just cause I like using 13):

Dre, Leader of the Cold Dawn - 3 pot cel
Jacob Bragg - 3 pot cel
Jimmy Dunn x2 - 4 POT CEL
Volker the Puppet Prince x2 - 5 pot CEL prince
Rake - 6 pot cel prince
Anvil - 6 POT CEL primogen
Bianca - 6 pot CEL 2 hand damage
Donal O'Connor - 8 POT CEL prince
Constanza Vinti - 8 POT CEL prince
Don Cruez the Idealist - 10 POT CEL justicar
Gwendolyn - 11 POT CEL inner circle +2 bleed
---
I think Gwendolyn is probably a bad idea after all. The theory
is that she can help pass votes, and she's the best for Minion Tapping
or Golconda'ing, but she can't play any of my P/J cards.

library (90):

masters:

3x Potence
2x Celerity
4x Haven Uncovered
5x Minion Tap
2x Golconda Inner Peace

actions:

4x Bum's Rush
3x Ambush
4x 5th Tradition Hospitality
3x Leather Jacket
Brujah Justicar
2x Anathema (accidentally lost one of those somewhere, used to have 3)
4x Archon

reactions:

3x 2nd Tradition Domain

combat:

12x Immortal Grapple
11x Torn Signpost
7x Blur
7x Taste of Vitae
2x Fists of Death
2x Pushing the Limit
3x Undead Strength
4x Flash
2x Amaranth
---

The idea behind the combat card split was to try and make fewer cards
per combat still do the work of putting vamps in torpor - eg superior
Signpost superior Grapple superior Blur for 9 damage, rather than
superior Signpost superior Grapple superior Undead Strength for 5,
press with Grapple, maybe Grapple again, hit for 3-5... In this way
I figured I could get away with reducing the proportion of combat
cards in the deck and putting other interesting stuff in. (used to
be about 60 combat/30 non including 13 masters.) At the same time,
the Archons are intended to reduce the need for as many Rush actions,
again to save space.

Problem is it's all still in theory, since I didn't even draw an Archon
let alone get to play one. I'd like to play this deck (but may well
end up playing its predecessor) at the tourney LSJ is running in Columbia
next weekend, but I'd have to be more confident that it would work well.
(Clearly I am obligated to play one combat deck or another, as it is
my sworn mission in life to defend the tourney viability of combat decks.)

Josh

I agree that, theoretically, banishment should have one of those two
conditions in order to keep it in line with the other cards, but game
theory aside, I am unconvinved that this is actually worth going to the
trouble of errataing.
Banishment is not, as you have asserted "just plain better" than KRC.
There is a subtle but important difference between costing pool and
actually doing "damage." KRC does damage. Pass enough, someone dies.
Banishment, on the other hand, only costs pool if your target brings out
the vampire again. A player at low pool may well take the opportunity
to suck the blood back to himself. An infinite number of banishments
will not slay a player. (of course, when he's out of vamps you can
bleed him to death, but when facing competetive decks you will rarely
have time to build up votes, then remove all of your preys vamps, then
bleed, and the odds of repeating the process with your next prey are
even worse.)
Banishment is, actually, slightly more "expensive" to use than KRC in
the sense that it will often require more votes to pass it. Huh?
What? Why? Consider: as has been noted, controlling the vote situation
is often difficult. In many cases you will need support from other
players in order to pass a vote. This is true for KRC as well, but the
difference is that KRC has 4 points to distribute so you can use one or
two to get someone else's prey and buy some votes. Banishment has one
target. Its only ever good for two people at a time (as opposed to
potentially four). You truly need vote dominance in order to actually
win with it.
Plus the best targets for banishment (large vamps) tend to have their
own votes to make your job more difficult.
Many cards could/should be tweaked minorly in order to make the game
more "perfect" but for most of them the "problem" is so small that it is
better to just leave the card as written because the game benefits even
more from keeping errata to a minimum. From what I've seen, Banishment
is one of those cases.

you will have more than one vampire on the first turn, if not 4.

vote deck (I certainly am not). You need odd combinations of cards, large
titled vampires, or a good supply of rares. However, as I have pointed out
before, this does not strike me as a problem, as it is completely analagous to
making a non Obf based S+B deck--it isn't going to be as good at pure S+B as an
Obf based S+B deck, so it needs to rely on whatever angle you get from not
being an Obf based S+B deck.

You are going to build a non Pre vote deck because you have a clever angle and
think that the clever angle will make it worth playing the deck even though it
will be less effective in an absolute sense than the Pre based deck. An example
of this (in a not vote sense) is my own Rush deck. I play a very effective
Pot/Obf small vampire based Rush deck, made out of Nosferatu. Conventional
wisdom would say that the deck would be better off built out of Brujah with
Pot/Cel, with all of my Behind Yous replaced with Flash. However, as I see it,
the Nosferatu have a better vampire selection (more small vampires that come
with POT) as well as access to the Storm Sewers, so I go the Nosferatu route.
In one on one combat, vs a Brujah deck, I'll probably lose. The rest of the
time, however, I kick ass.

A non Pre based vote deck will have trouble if sitting next to a pure Pre vote
deck, yeah. However, it won't always be sitting near such a deck, and in the
appropriate environement, it will do great. If your local environement consists
of nothing but severe, Pre based vote decks, your Nosferatu Prince deck
probably won't do all that well. Bring one into a low vote environement, or
into a blind tournament, and you'll be perfectly compettetive.

I don't think I'm confused at all. I see my deck as a vote deck because
it uses political actions. modifiers, and vote reactions as a major part

> Your deck was effective because it used the Parthenon
> to generate 2 Anarch Revolts a turn.

That *is* the main part of its strategy, but you are now oversimplifying.
The deck works as a whole. In order to ensure that I will benefit from
these Anarchs, I must damage my prey early and fast. This is essential.

> The one AR/MRC combo you did pull
> off proabably didn't have much effect on the game as I doubt your prey
> would have lasted more than another turn.

At the rate you were bleeding me, a delay of one or two turns in ousting
my prey might have cost me the game, as I would have been ousted first by
your bleeds and my own Anarchs. Seven pool loss to one's prey is never
anything to underestimate. Timing and speed is all-important in an Anarch
Revolt deck.

Sure, my prey would probably have been doomed in any event, but what good
is that to me if you are the one that gets the vp after ousting me?

In retrospect, however, I wish I had divided the pool-loss equally between
prey and grand-prey, as I might have ousted 2 Methuselahs in this case.
But that is hindsight. Other mistakes, I wish I had bled for the edge
prior to casting the Malkavian Justicar vote.

Besides which, I "pulled off" multiple AR/MRC combos. The ones that did
not get me an automatically-passed offensive vote had other valuable
effects: They kept the ARs in play longer and caused my opponents to
waste additional minion actions to try to remove them, when they needed to
be racing me *real* fast to oust their own prey first. The Conservative
Agitations that I did not pass still had the effect of intimidating people
out of burning the Anarch Revolts.

Anarch Revolt, BTW, *is* a vote card, and AR/MRC is a vote combination.
That makes my deck a sort of political deck even without the offensive
vote cards like conservative agitation.

> The point is that as a combo,
> AR/MRC is not a consistent method to pass votes.

True, but unlike vote reactions like Dread Gaze, it serves as a dual
purpose. It can be used defensively to prevent hostile votes from passing,
as well as to gain enormous benefit from those that do pass. I don't
think you have given fair consideration to its benefits.

Calling it "unreliable" is misleading. Sure, it is "unreliable" but in
spite of this, it is 100% effective every time it is played. While its
effects may be unpredictable (appropriate for a Malkavian deck), it's
effect always benefits you if you play it during a referendum that you
would not otherwise wish to pass. You either stop the vote, or you get a
free vote of your own.

> Whether your deck is
> able to win because it generates 2 AR cards a turn is irrelevant to this
> point.

Except that that is not in itself sufficient to ensure victory in this
type of deck. Besides which, those AR cards are vote cards, making my
deck political if I choose to do anything to defend them (which I did).

We are going to keep arguing in circles, saying that each-other's points
are "irrelevant". Everything you say is true, but I still think you are
missing the big picture. As best as I can recall the original main point
of this discussion is whether non-presence vote decks are effective. I
maintain that they are, and you are maintaining otherwise. I agree that
this deck is not the best example to prove my case, but, on the other
hand, it certainly does not benefit yours -- and you are the one that
brought it up. We are discussing a single non-presence vote deck that
failed to win, but also failed to lose, in the context of a single game.
This neither proves nor disproves the effectiveness of non-presence vote
decks or of Malkavian Rider Clause. First off, the deck did indeed "work"
to a marginal extent; second, cards that don't work in one deck might work
better in another; third, this is just one example of a zillion possible
non-presence vote decks.

> > table. It is not a fair testing ground for the general effectiveness of
> > the Malkavian Rider Clause in terms of passing votes.
>
> It is definitely a "fair testing ground" to determine whether a AR/MRC
> combo is an effective means to pass votes. Clearly, it is not. In fact,

fails, it serves to defeat opposing votes. It is a great non-presence
political card.

Dread Gaze may be more effective at defeating votes you don't like, but
when it fails to achieve this purpose it does not have the wonderful side
effect of letting you automatically pass your own votes.

Besides which, I did not rely on the Rider Clause alone to pass votes. I
used a combination of Surprise Influence, and bleeding for the edge to
cause the vote to pass after the Rider Clause was played. I also hoped to
put a Justicar on the table, which failed because I foolishly failed to
bleed for the edge first, and got defeated by a Dread Gaze at Superior by
a margin of 1 vote. There were other tricks up my sleeve that I
unfortunately never got to try.

You are tempting me to try the deck again, though I am sure no-one at the

No, no, you are missing the point of what I am looking for. What I wanted, from
the get go, was a deck that used an absurd amount of one card that:

A) Is so effective (in a grand sense, not a narrow sense) that it wins on a
more than reliable basis,

B) Has no common and/or incredibly obvious crippling weaknesses,

C) Requires decks be designed specifically to beat it, or die.

What I was not looking for was a deck that had an absurd number of one card
that:

A) Is really good at one particular thing, but is easily trounced in most other
common situations,

B) Isn't capable of getting VPs in a reliable fashion (i.e is not a deck that
can actually win).

The 50 DotB deck, while novel and kind of funny, does not fulfil any of the
points in the first list and fulfils all of the points in the second list. A
deck with weenie ANI vamps and 50 DotB will completely shut down a Rush deck
and will cause a great deal of trouble to a zero stealth horde bleed deck,
sure. However, it seems highly unlikely that it will be able to oust anyone in
any timely fashion, will be quicky destroyed by a quick S+B or vote predator,
will suffer from hideous hand jam ("Look. I have 7 DotB in my hand, but no one
wants to block my bleeds for 1..."), and will be hard pressed to get any VPs,
let alone win a table (or a tournament for that matter), and will run out of
cards very quickly. Not an overly effective deck in my book.

1x Dani 2cap ani
